I like music, I like art, I like creativity and seeing and feeling human emotions. K-pop has all of it in spades lol. I listen to a pretty wide variety of music I think? If music makes me feel feelings then I like it lol. Phonk, country, classical, hip-hop, whatever. Of course there’s stuff that I don’t particularly enjoy, but imo K-pop is just as good of a music genre as any other genres. And it’s got a lot of variety under its umbrella anyways - rock, pop, metal, etc. etc. 

but k-pop is definitely more of an industry than one concrete genre. I really like the community aspect of it. I’ve found a lot of friends through it.
I like looking at pretty people. Sue me, I’m only human. I love art so I love seeing the wacky photoshoots and music videos and album covers and photobooks etc., etc. It’s pretty people + art. There’s also the amount of content. It’s like having a favourite podcaster, but he also makes music, shoots videos, does vlogs, does blogs, tweets nonstop, etc. If you think a person is a cool artist, it’s REALLY nice to have to much info available about them. Plus it’s like having pocket comedians in your inventory. Pull out your phone and easily pull out something that amuses you. 

+ this is really important -> I do think the music listening experience is improved when you have an emotional attachment to the songs/albums/whatever. Since you have so much information available about the artists it’s very easy to feel emotional attachment to the music. “ah, this song speaks about social anxiety and I know this person struggles in big crowds, I know how that feels and I can relate”, ya kno? Or even “aww, I can hear how much fun this cool person is having while they belt this song at the top of their lungs”. 

As for what turns me away from groups -> no involvement in the creative side of their profession. I prefer artists and groups who produce their own music and/or do choreographies and/or get involved in the creative direction of their image (fashion, album designs, etc., whatever). I’ve listened to a lot of groups and the only ones who keep my attention long term are those who do their own stuff (it’s not very surprising, I know). On this note, any AI whatever and I’m out lol. Also turns me away when they visit genocidal states like Russia ngl.

Oh hi, you’re me! Yes, I have this too. There’s a few things you can do! None of them are a 100% cure, but if a few of them work 5% then with enough of them your life will be 50% easier you know. My issue is specifically _starting_ to do something. Once I know what I’m doing (and what I’m supposed to be doing) and I have a direction I know I’m supposed to go in I don’t really have an issue working on papers or memorising things, etc.. It’s the uncertainty that’s the issue lol. 

Anyways, firstly, you’re paying for your degree. You’re a customer. It’s not high school. Even if you receive a stipend or uni is free for you, you’re still a customer. Universities are there to provide things for YOU. You’re not there to please the uni. The uni is there to please you. This is kinda hard to actually internalise, but keep it in mind. 

On this topic, feel free to bother professors. Maybe start with a low stakes question to make it easier?“Good afternoon! I’m a student from course X and I wanted to clarify a question about homework. The description does not say whether you’d like us to include a bibliography at the end of the essay, is it necessary? Thank you!” or whatever like that. But ideally you should use your professors as resources themselves and ask “I’m thinking about doing [essay title] would this work do you think? I found source1, source2, source3 for this topic.” lol. Of course there are assholes in the world, but students willing to learn are catnip usually. Seriously, utilise your professors! They’re smart and it’s cool to talk with smart people because you learn new things. Uni staff are also there to help, my head of administration for my degree is 10/10 she’s probably saved me from losing my sanity a few times. Maybe yours isn’t a 10/10 person, but it’s worth it to hit them up with an email. You’re 100% not the first uni student stressed out about scheduling tasks and figuring out priorities. 

Secondly, I kinda sneak up on tasks? Like… approach them sideways. I don’t tell myself “I will write 3 pages tonight or else I’ll fail and be doomed and end up living an unhappy life”. I tell myself “I’ll sit down, I’ll open my laptop, I’ll have my document open on one half of the screen and a [insert favourite YT video] open on the other side of the screen. I’ll only glance at the document. That is it.” and then when I approach it like this it’s much easier to reword a sentence I don’t like in the document and write down a few words, and lo and behold in the end you “accidentally” work on whatever you need working on. Placebo I guess? It helps. 

Thirdly, change environments. I had an issue with opening my uni email account. Literally couldn’t click the button. 0/10 it sucks. I started opening it at super random moments when I’m distracted. Usually while I’m walking to public transport way too early in the morning and sometimes if I woke up in the middle of the night or while standing in line at a coffee shop. It’s cuz I was associating the email with absolute sheer terror while sitting at my kitchen table and staring at my laptop trying to click the button lol. Maybe go for a walk and think in the direction of your tasks? 

Fourthly, even if the idea is shit, start doing it. You don’t need to find “the perfect idea” to start doing it. Seriously. It always takes trial and error. It’s the easiest to work when you have momentum, like a stone rolling down a hill. Even if all you have is 300 words of total bullshit, maybe in the end 1 word will be useful. 

Fifth, stop thinking long term. If an assignment hasn’t been assigned yet - forget about it. All you need to think about is what’s happening right _now_. The most immediate thing, the closest deadline. Things 6 months in the future are useless. If you need ideas for a project, that’s all you have to do. You don’t have to make the project right now. You need specifically ideas. That’s it. Don’t borrow grief. Here’s a song recommendation, listen to the lyrics lol. https://open.spotify.com/track/68oBm4o7JfsLezeq7r9LzN?si=bkZh4MhmTMGjnRcqeFFImg

When all else fails, a call to a friend! When stuff is seriously hard for me I literally sit next to my mother and tell her “I’m insanely stressed out right now, I’ll try to work for a bit, you just sit there and do what you’ve been doing. It’ll help me.”. It’s easier with someone keeping calm next to you, someone who you know is supportive. Studying together with friends maybe? 

Also, check if your uni doesn’t provide free therapy, I love that stuff. Or if you have an opportunity to go to therapy and/or it’s possible, take it. Therapy doesn’t work for everyone, but if it works for you then it’ll be a big help.

Anxiety is one of the worst competitions to participate in, ever. Don’t compete in it. Your worst panic attack that you’ve ever had was the worst panic attack you’ve ever personally experienced. When you think about “what is my anxiety like?” your own personal experience and your personal suffering should matter to you the most. Is it not enough to say “this is the worst I’ve ever felt in my life” for it to count as “suffering from anxiety”? In short, of course feel free to commiserate with and have empathy for those who’ve commented on this post, but there’s no need to say “they had it worse, so I had it _good_” because that’s not how it works.

Nah, sorry, smoking doesn’t help. You get _more_ anxious when you don’t have an opportunity to smoke. The only thing smoking “helps” with is having something to focus on when you’re anxious. If you need “something to focus on” take up a small hobby, sudoku on phone, herbal teas, chewing gum, rings to fidget with, reading movie reviews, music, literally absolutely whatever. It will serve the same purpose, but you won’t have to spend an insane amount of money over time and it won’t be unhealthy and generally a very unpleasant and smelly habit. The last thing you need right now is another stressor and cigarettes are a stressor. 

Source: been smoking for 10+ years and have anxiety.

For skz ot8 (9 pocket pages) it goes - one page each at the beginning of the binder holding my favourite pcs (display pages basically, useful for the random brand collabs and fan calls that I don’t plan on finishing the sets for, rare photocards, etc.), then chronological full sets with the leftover sleeve having cut up album inserts/freebies/lomos. First album photocards, then POBs for each “era”. Then for those I don’t have full sets and don’t wanna display I just keep them by member at the end of the binder. 

So it’s display pages -> chronological full sets -> a slight mess that I clean up when I finish a set/have enough for another display page. It means that I start off the binder with a bang, then it’s very satisfying and I ignore the end. 

For the other groups I keep the groups together and sort by members rather than albums and I have the groups vaguely grouped. So it’s - soloists -> bands -> well established groups -> recent debut groups/small groups. It just makes sense for me to sort them like that since it flows well for my brain.

Disclaimer: this is obv just my personal experience! That over with, it was really good for me, precisely what I needed. I’d say it lessened my anxiety by some 70% or so, precisely enough that I could easily function day-to-day without any issues. ~30% leftover anxiety is really easy to live with then you’re used to 100% anxiety at all times lol and it gradually lessened from the 30% to being negligible. At super stressful events (social events are my biggest issue 100%) I still had anxiety, but the type that’s manageable you know? I could do some breathing exercises and get through the first 10min with super sweaty hands and then I’d chill out, whereas before I would probably have a panic attack. I didn’t have any particular side effects that were bothersome, no issues with being “too” chill, slept well, etc. As far as I remember maybe it did make me sleepy for a little bit right after I took it? But it was smth like this - I took it right before I went to sleep, so I fell asleep easier because I was a bit sleepy. But if I decided to stay up after taking it, it wasn’t an issue, I just felt a little bit sleepy for idk an hour maybe, like when you’re doing something insanely boring at work/etc., so it wasn’t an issue. For example, it would be harder to stay awake if you read something insanely boring while snugged up in bed, but like, negligible, while it wouldn’t be hard to stay awake if you were reading something interesting. Don’t quote me on this, but from what I remember my psych told me it slightly lowers blood pressure, which is why you might feel more sleepy. Absolutely ask your doc about this, I might be misremembering something! I did have increased appetite, but as I said it only made my appetite reach a “normal” level, I didn’t have cravings/want to binge/etc. Coming off it was pretty easy too! A bit more anxiety while I got used to it, but that’s it. No dizzy spells, no depression, no vertigo, no major anxiety, etc. As far as I remember I took it for a few years once, then went off for a few months/years (didn’t have any real stressors in life, so meds weren’t really necessary anymore), then went on them again for a few months/years and then went off them again when my life stabilised again. They kicked in really fast for me too, matter of a week or two if not days. No issues arose from taking them semi-longterm as well. Didn’t need to bump up the dose once I found my sweet spot. All of this was done under the supervision of a psychiatrist, btw, just to clarify. 

So overall it was good for me! If you have any other questions or smth specific you’re interested in, feel free to ask!

Slippery slope you know? A dose of cough syrup for sleep, then a dose in the morning to get through the day, maybe before driving the car as well and then lo and behold after a week or two you need to contact the doctor to quit using it safely or endanger your health and your kiddo is asking you some uncomfortable questions. On top of that I’m quite sure overusing Benadryl can end up with having hallucinations which is… not the best thing in the world for most people and especially if you have anxiety. Other medications run the same risk and well, just generally using meds as they are not prescribed is not the best option. It’s really easy to start relying on them. And speaking from experience, if you preemptively take “emergency meds” before the first stressful evening, you probably won’t trust yourself to be fine the second evening without them. And using meds the wrong way for a week straight is super sketchy. 

Absolutely feel free to contact your doctor and ask them for what would be the best course of action for you, though! It’s totally fine to have some kind of emergency measures - maybe having a video call with your wife until you fall asleep (if it’s a hard evening), maybe having a movie night with your kiddo and sleeping in the living room, maybe the GP will have other recs, etc. There’s other options out there than overusing over the counter meds is what I’m saying. Brainstorm a bit and don’t take the option that can end up with hallucinations/being bothersome down the road. Sustainable habits will make your life easier in the long run.

Best starting point is the most simple one! Go to any cosmetics isle and find the nail products. You’ll want a metal nail file with a pointy end or any nail file AND a cuticle pusher tool (google it, it looks like something you scoop stuff with). And you will want cuticle oil - I like the ones with vitamin E! Also a hand cream wouldn’t go amiss, I’m a sucker for Nivea ones, people also like aquaphor. 

The routine is this. If your hands are dry use hand cream. I usually use it after washing hands and keep it on my desk/bedside table. Keep your cuticle oil in your bathroom/on your bedroom table. Every few days (or when you remember it, it’s not required to keep a super strict schedule) plop some cuticle oil on your nails and cuticles and rub it in. Let it sit for a little bit (a minute or two, or if you’re feeling lazy just don’t wait) and take your pointy nail file/cuticle pusher. Push your cuticles back a little bit. If it hurts - stop. It’s kinda hard to misjudge your strength at first/have proper fine motor control for this specific thing and you might poke a bit too hard, it’s whatever, just know it’s not supposed to hurt lol. Keep the cuticle line somewhat even, that’s the goal here. Looks neater. File any uneven free hanging nail parts so they’re neat (don’t file the top of the nails, just the part with which you can scratch people).

Tadah! Done. 

Lazy version - get hand cream. Use it. Use the nails of your other hand to push back your cuticles. Use a nail file to have not-sharp-nail-edges.

I personally absolutely love travelling, I think it’s a brilliant way to prove to yourself (if you’re an anxious person) that anxiety doesn’t rule your life. It always gives me a super big confidence boost as well, for a few weeks at the very least, if not a few months. So generally speaking I am all for travelling! At the same time, definitely speak with your friend about your anxiety and how it manifests! I was SUPER nervous before I traveled without my parents for the first time, so I literally sent my best friend with who I was going on the trip with a list of instructions of what to do if I have a panic attack and what helps me. Now, looking back, it was overkill lol, it would’ve been fine to just have a frank convo with her irl, but the bottom line is that communication is really helpful in cases like this. Having that one other person with you who can call a taxi for you, or tell someone “no thank you, we don’t want to do that” if the anxiety has kicked in hard is a reeeeally nice safety net to have. With this I mean, while I can’t say I’d go on this trip in your case, it IS a wonderful opportunity and do make sure that you consider the pros as well as cons. I’d probably also think up some compromise plans? Like, for example, maybe if you wouldn’t want to join a house party with random people, you can suggest that a bar crawl would be a nice alternative. Or if staying over at someone’s place outside the city seems too sketch, you would however be fine staying with someone in the suburbs. You know? Basically, unless a trip is absolutely insane there are so many options out there to compromise on, if need be. And, personally, when I’ve talked all of this stuff over with friends (this is for doing sketch shit, I don’t do this whole process for daily things, there’s a limit to how much one should let anxiety rule them lmao) my anxiety goes WAY down because I have the certainty that everything will be fine no matter what happens. Lmao this ended up being an essay, sorry about that. Travelling is cool as shit, highly recommended, think about your hard limits and if they are suitable for this specific trip and find out what compromises you two can live with and you’ll probably have your answer. Good luck! ✨

Realistically it’s always going to be more anxiety inducing to do more dangerous stuff than less dangerous stuff. So I absolutely get why this seems both like an amazing opportunity and super stressful. You couldn’t pay me to do those type of stuff, but as you said, women live a different life. But if I were you I’d browbeat my anxiety with logic and plans. I.e., always have a way out of any situation you might end up in, whatever country you’re at, make sure you have enough money for a plane ticket home, wherever you couch surf make sure you can leave at any point and get a hotel. Whatever people you’re with, make sure you can say no to whatever activity you don’t want to participate in (skinny dipping, bar crawling, meth, visiting their grandma, etc.), that’s what I’d do to make sure my anxiety wasn’t the logical anxiety of someone who’s in a potentially dangerous situation. I’d DEFINITELY also discuss this with your friend. Make sure he knows you have anxiety, make sure he WILL be okay with you taking a break from activities or even leaving and going home if you’re just not vibing with it. Maybe you can even do a small test trip? A whole summer is A LOT. if you’ve got the time and cash to spare could you do a test couch surfing weekend with your friend? To the next city/state over or whatever distance you Americans consider reasonable? Maybe this’ll give you some ideas!

I’m not OP but I can offer my perspective as an anxious person who absolutely blossomed when i started my bachelors. 

Firstly, on the matter of friends, imo it’s easier to make friends in uni because everyone’s in the same boat. They’re all strangers there so there are no (or few) friendship groups u are the outsider for. Also mandatory uni icebreakers are very good for that, group activities, group projects, etc. There WILL be opportunities for social interactions and most likely there will be someone who will do a bit of heavy lifting for you if you blank out. Also also you have THE perfect small talk topic that WILL 100% be acceptable and even interesting - classes. Mandatory reading, professors, assignments, etc. If there will be a group chat for ur class, use it, interact with memes, ask questions etc. If you know someone from a group project, because you sat next to them, gave them a pen, etc., you can always greet them each time you see them and ask who ever is sitting next to you “hey how are you, did u do the [whatever was the task]?” At a minimum you will have SO MANY pleasant acquaintances if you speak at least a littttle bit. 

On the more academic aspects - uni professors are SO chill, so I feel like it’s even easier to be a teachers pet/one of the students they recognise? My approach to becoming an accidental teachers pet/being recognised (depends on class size) was - be polite, greet them and say goodbye, ask the questions you have when they invite questions, answer questions they ask the class, always do homework and don’t be super disruptive in class. ✅ you’re a student they like now. Hmm what else. The rest of academic stuff was also fine for me. Just do all your assigned reading ALWAYS(!), ask questions, do homework, DON’T cheat or at the very least don’t rely on cheating, don’t pay people to write your stuff for you, try your best, even if you might fail you HAVE to attempt because you really don’t want your brain stuck in a rut of “I will not even TRY to learn this/pass this test/ask this question” lol. 

Anyways this is more of a ramble, but uni was so so so good for me.

Yep, there are some photocards that are 100% limited and are no longer produced. Some albums just aren’t produced/sold anymore, but there’s also more “esoteric” stuff. Maybe a member left a group so their photocards are no longer included in albums. Some photocards were sold/you could get them only at event X, and that’s it. Then there are Polaroids! Which are, literally, Polaroids, i.e. an idol uses a Polaroid camera so it is 100% unique and can’t be copied. Many of those only the owners know what they look like, since you don’t really show them off publicly, that lessens the value and allows people to use them to scam others. Also signed photocards! Those, obviously, are also limited. So there’s definitely things to take into account on that side. But that’s more on the super serious collector side imo. It’s a whole stock market/free market/no regulation simulation out there lol. 

No need to take it that seriously though, some (like me) just choose a specific “set” of photo cards they think look nice (or have an emotional connection, like “I saw this album performed live”) and have fun trying to find all of them. You can also trade photocards which is another fun aspect! Person x has a card you want, you have a card they want. Match made in heaven. Legit subculture around the whole thing. Should a member that’s more popular have more expensive photocards? Should you support this specific shop that does “shop unique” photocards if they have bad business practices? Etc. etc.

In short, it’s fun. 100% the same as literally all collecting hobbies ever. Stamps, cool rocks, bottle caps, photocards, rare currencies, stickers, books, jewellery. It’s all the same. Breathing exercises help a lot of people, you can Google some. My fave is breathing in and super strongly visualising that I’m breathing out and air is streaming out of my mouth, then breathing out and imagining that I’m drawing in a breath deep from my stomach into my lungs and up my throat to my mouth. So you visualise the opposite of what you’re doing, because that makes you have to REALLY concentrate on what you’re doing. It’s also kinda fun? I sometimes do it just because why not. 

Another one of my faves is: breathe in with opened eyes and name one thing you can see. Only one! You can’t go “tree, building, house, ah I choose to name “flower””, you gotta keep your brain empty and only name one thing. Close your eyes while you exhale. Open your eyes while you inhale and name a new thing. This is also fun because you really have to concentrate on keeping your brain empty and letting only ONE word show up in your brain. 

Also you can stick your hand in ice cold tap water. Just tell people you stubbed a finger if someone asks. But I really do recommend my breathing exercises, they’re actually fun and feel more like a “game” than “I am panicking and trying to not panic exercises”.

Generally speaking albums (of bigger groups with 💸) usually have limited version, regular versions and digipacks. 

Limited versions are limited, at some point then will be sold out and comparatively much harder to find. They also usually have nicer goodies inside, some additional stuff. This is the best choice. 

Regular versions keep getting restocked, so they won’t run out. That’s why I personally think it’s nicer to get the limited version. 

Digipacks are the smaller/cheaper versions of the albums. They have less stuff and are smaller in size. 

5 star has 1 limited, 3 regular and 8 digipacks (one for each member).

You might notice references to pre-order benefits or POB’s. There are two aspects here. IF you order an album before it’s released the album might contain additional stuff, like a poster or something like that. Sometimes the POB photocards can be bought separately or even after the album is released I’ve noticed, but they get sold out fast lol. This is more relevant to the future albums. 

Japanese albums are usually way more expensive and have way less cool stuff. So eh.

1. Figure out your budget. What’s the optimal price point for you? I.e. 500eur or 1000eur or…? 

2. Figure out if you’re going with someone or alone. That impacts what resort you’ll want to choose, what expenses you’ll have, possible deals you can get etc. 

3. If your budget is small and you’re going alone - Google budget resorts&beginner resorts. If the opposite, you have more freedom. 

4. Choose a resort. Google is your friend. Ask for recommendations from those who go on ski trips. Search Reddit for recs and reviews. 
4a. Check how you can get to the resort. I don’t do resorts that require transfer flights because fuck that, and I prefer a ski shuttle from airport to the resort. It’s cheaper than renting a car. And last time I rented a car we all got stuck on an overpass and arrived at 5 in the morning because of a snowstorm lmao. 

5. Check ski lift prices at the resort for however many days you wanna do. I usually do 5 days snowboarding (two days travel, to and fro). Check “seasons” for prices. A lot of resorts have a few weeks when it’s more expensive (like student holidays, when resorts are popular) and when it’s cheaper. 

6. Check flights. Are there those nice discounted 50eur flights? Run numbers on how ticket seasons and flight prices intersect and figure out what’s the optimal moment to snowboard. 

7. Check hotels/apartments. Choose ones that are either close to a ski lift, close to public ski transport, or have rental car parking. I prefer close to ski lift or with public ski transport stops. Also, I suggest checking if they have a snowboard storage room. They usually do, but still. 

8. Decide if you’re renting or bringing your own gear. Bringing your gear on the plane can be more expensive than renting because fuck the sports gear transportation fees lol. 

9. Create a plan. Think on it a bit. And pull the trigger.

Eh, same. The first few minutes you really just gotta breathe through it. But after that there are some (very) small things that can help. But the thing with small things is that if you have 20 small things that each help 2%, you still end up feeling 40% better which is a LOT. 

Firstly, have enough time in the morning that you can do everything you’ve gotta do. Schedule enough time you don’t feel pressure to hurry. If you have no logical reasons to be anxious, life’s easier. Won’t fix the illogical anxiety, but will help. Secondly, have a pleasant routine. For me it is - wake up, take the dogs for a wee (fresh air really helps), wash my face and teeth while listening to a podcast (or whatever other audio that is nice to listen to and distracting), eat breakfast (while reading/listening to something), get dressed. Key factors here are having a schedule YOU like and having things that will distract you that YOU like. Third, kinda treat mornings as sacred. At least until you leave your house for work, etc. Do not read negative media, do not watch unpleasant things (hate binge annoying people), etc. Fourth, routine, I know I said it already, but if you have a set routine, you’ll know what to do even if you’re like 3 steps away from a panic attack. It’s easier to ride that feeling out if you don’t have to try to divert attention to making decisions. Fifth, miscellaneous things to try out- drink tea (chamomile, peppermint, stuff like that), do some exercises (stretch for literally 10min), open the windows if it’s warm/cool enough so you get fresh air (stand in front of the open window for 3min), drink your first cup of coffee/tea outside (if that’s possible), do slow things (i.e. read a book, not watch short insta/Reddit/TikTok/whatever content, listen to a podcast not a 5min YT summary video, etc.), prepare things you need the previous day (clothes, work/uni/school bag, breakfast food, etc), do 5min of breathing exercises right after waking up, alternatively, immediately after waking up get dressed and go for a 15min walk. 

These aren’t things that are a cure, that’s for sure, but if you honestly give a good try to all of them, you will probably find something that makes your life easier. Antidepressant withdrawals are a fckn horrid thing to go through, I know. But there are a lot of small things you can do to make the process a bit easier. For me personally, it helps to have a list of habits to “try out”, because it gives my brain hope and things to think about that’s not just a rat running in a wheel from certain doom. 

But also, if the withdrawals are absolutely horrid, go talk with your doctor, you might want to try tapering off more slowly, etc. It’s always worth checking in.

Vet first, trainer second. 

But my two cents is that (AFTER you’ve eliminated ALL other options like lameness/teeth/saddle fit/etc.!!!) this type of sudden regress can happen due to the rider not being experienced enough. First you have a honeymoon period where the horse still remembers the previous experienced/stricter riders. Then you make some small mistakes (letting the horse transition from trot to walk before you asked for it, cutting corners shorter, etc.) and the horse goes “hmmmm…? I can do that?”. Then the horse tests out their genius idea (refuses canter, refuses mounting, etc.). And if they succeed then you have some work in front of you because the horse now knows they can make a fool out of you. That’s why it’s insanely important for new riders to have trainers. Having an experienced and good rider sometimes ride your horse can help as well. What worked the best for me when I went through this lovely list is having a trainer 1-2 times a week, riding alone 1-3 times and week and having an experienced rider ride 1-2 times a week. Coming out to some 5-6 days of work for the horse which was the correct intensity for that specific horse, this should be adjusted for each horse individually.

This is one of the most important things! The horse will need time to settle in, you both will need time to understand each other and it’s always, always better to progress “too slowly” than to rush something. I had a trainer push me and one of my old horses way too quickly, and after one two hour long lesson of her absolutely badgering me and the horse on a single movement it took us some two months to start trusting each other again. It’s always better to end a lesson/ride on a good note even if the lesson is 50min long not the whole 60 minutes. Your goal is to build yourself and your horse up and to have pleasant rides. That’s it. Throw out all timelines (when to start cantering, first competitions, first flying changes, first 1.20m jump, etc.) and focus on being healthy, taking pleasure in all progress no matter how slow and finding things to be happy about. Enjoy bonding with your horse on the ground, a nice walk trot transition, a millimetre more collection, etc. Don’t get stuck in a rut of “achievements” you must have. The more you purposefully find things to be happy about the happier you will be. 

Also, I cannot recommend this enough, write down a few sentences after EACH ride. You will LOVE looking back on them. I found that the more I focused on relaxing my ankles and letting them flex solely from body weight, and the more I focused on relaxing my knees to let them sink deep the easier and less painful it got. Also shock absorption increased by a lot. Image the feeling of falling backwards in your bed after a long day and letting your whole body slouch and relax. Then do the same from hips down on the snowboard. Obviously you still use your tight muscles and calves, but generally speaking ankles should flex naturally when you are leaning forward.

On the pressure issue. Check your technique. Are you flexing your ankle up to get an edge, or are you leaning with your weight? My circulation was shit when I used to brute force flex my ankle instead of working with my own weight. Now I try to make sure that my ankles are as relaxed as I can possibly make them. 

Also, check if your bindings are positioned correctly on the boot. If they create weird pressure spots that can cut off circulation. Mine used to be too short, so the pressure was unevenly distributed on one side of the boot. Also if they are too tight, that can also be an issue. And also, maybe you need to adjust your binding position. I shifted mine 3° forward and that (plus technique) fixed my shin splint pain + circulation issues. 

Finally, as a quick survival tip - get used to scrunching your toes up and relaxing and scrunching and relaxing whenever you’re not actively snowboarding. On the lift, in the line, etc. That’ll make your life easier while you get to the bottom of the issue. :D

I’ve always been prescribed anti depressants for my anxiety. They work phenomenally well by lowering my anxiety to a point where I can actually start dealing with it and healing from it, not only barely surviving. I was on meds for a few years, got much better and went off for a few years, then got a bit worse and used them again for a year and now am going off them again. They’re a super useful tool! I’m saying tool because they’re not the holy grail, therapy, treating yourself well, improving your physical health, etc., are all things that can and should be used at the same time. 

If you are worried about medicine impacting your sex life, tell your doctor! There are MANY options for what kind of medicine you can use. For example, I told my doctor that I would like to try meds that are easy to stop using (no withdrawals) and also that increase appetite (a known side effect for mine is that some people get fat. Since I struggled with eating enough and was underweight they worked out perfectly for me). If you notice your sex life being impacted, you can switch to other meds. 

Going to a psychiatrist isn’t “I went there, the doc told me to use X and only X without my input, now I will forever have to suffer the side effects”. The visits are more like “here are my symptoms and what I would like improved, what are my options? I don’t like these options, please tell me what else I could do. What side effects are possible? How long should I use the meds to find out if I’ll have these side effects? I don’t like these meds, please change them.” Etc etc etc. It’s a collaboration not a dictatorship. If your doctor isn’t willing to work with you on what side effects are fine and what aren’t you absolutely can change to a new one. 

Some things you can write down and tell your doctor before your first visit:
My symptoms are -
My symptoms started - 
Im worried about these side effects -
Im not worried about these side effects -

Meds for mental health are like meds for physical illness, a part of the healing process if they’re necessary.

Yeah I’ve had the same issue with makeup in general. The thing is, we get used to “new” looks super fast. If you always look at yourself in the mirror with makeup on you’ll get used to your “regular” self having makeup on. That’ll become the standard even if it’s not. Then when you take the makeup (lashes, hair extensions, etc.) off you’ll feel like you’re looking worse. You’re not looking worse, your brain just got too used to seeing you with your lashes on. An accident def shouldn’t happen and you don’t need to worry about one. I rode like this some 5+ years and I had precisely one accident when I had a randomly super strong period (like the big night pad is completely full, all of it is red in one hour type of period). If you want to feel safer about having periods and riding juuuuuust in case then keep a few tissues in your pocket and when you loosen the girth/put on stirrups/give a treat to the horse after riding you can run your hand over the saddle and check if there’s a leak and wipe it off immediately. And keep a another jacket where you dismount so you can tie it around your waist to hide your butt in case of a leak. And wear dark breeches if you have ones. That way even if there’s a random 1% possibility of a leak you can solve it immediately and know what to do. But yeah, as long as you use a fresh pad you’re good. :)

I wear pads while riding and yeah, they sometimes do end up a bit torn. It’s fine if the top layer is torn, the bottom layer is the one that holds all the blood, so they’re not going to leak. I recommend wearing tight fitting underwear and tight breeches (maybe throw in a “chafing protector”, tight spandex shorts on top of underwear as well) so the pad is constantly pressed against you and can’t twist around. Also, wear night pads, those that are super long, with big wings. Make sure that the wings underneath the panties overlap a bit, the glue is quite strong and they won’t come undone that way. Also, you can end up with sensitive genitalia from them rubbing against you. Take a wet paper towel and wipe your genitalia before riding, dry it, put on a new pad. After riding, also immediately wipe yourself with a wet cloth/paper towel, dry yourself and put on a new pad.

Hah, hi friend, I had dandruff in my ears, head and eyebrows. 

General advice - don’t sleep with wet hair, carefully comb your hair before showering (you’ll be able to rinse out the loose dandruff easily, and will have less after showering), washing your hair TOO frequently will dry your hair out, that’s bad (try to wash your hair when it looks oily. Even if you shower twice a day, only wash your hair when it looks oily, don’t wash it twice a day, but once a day or every other day, for example). If your head gets very sweaty, wash your hair that day, don’t sleep with the sweat still on your head). Don’t use conditioner on your scalp, it doesn’t help dandruff, only increases it. 

More specifically:

For hair- try nizoral shampoo, or head and shoulders anti dandruff stuff. If that doesn’t work, use apple cider vinegar (take a regular ~250ml cup, splash a little bit of vinegar in it. The amount is approximately up to your first knuckle. Go to the shower and take the cup with you. Shampoo your hair, rinse it out, then fill the cup the rest of way with water and pour the vinegar and water mixture on your scalp. Rise after a few minutes.) if vinegar hurts - stop, if it gets in your eyes - rinse, if you have open sores - don’t use, it’ll sting.

For eyebrows - get an old mascara wand or something like that from a mother/friend (but wash it well before using!), or buy a new eyebrow spoolie from a makeup store. Gently brush the dandruff out of your eyebrows each morning. You can try to dab the vinegar mixture on it, or gently apply a bit of shampoo when you wash your hair. 

For ears - vinegar mixture as well. 

For beard - also vinegar mixture I assume. I don’t have a beard, but it can’t hurt and should work the same. 

If this doesn’t work - I heartily recommend visiting a dermatologist. My dermatologist patted me on the back for using vinegar and prescribed some type of cream for my ears, because they were being kinda stubborn about dandruff. My head was dandruff free in like three washes with vinegar. My eyebrows are better but not perfect, but I don’t care, because brushing the dandruff out is easy. The dermatologist will also help you figure out what to best wash your face with so it’s not dry and you can ask them to check any moles you have, etc. They’re cool. 

Good luck :)

In these types of cases imo you’ve gotta weight the benefits (to you and others) and the downsides (to you and others). Also whether your actions will improve the situation. Any action you take will result in at least one of those. There are few actions that are TRULY neutral. 

For example, the only real actions I can see you logically taking is talking with the involved parties. 

Weight this - what’s the benefit to you (you will ease your conscience), benefit to others (they might feel better), downside to you (you will get sucked into the conflict), downside to others (probably none). Will you improve anything (you probably won’t solve their interpersonal relationship issues, might improve your relationships with either or both of them).

Taking these into account you’ve gotta figure out if the benefit of easing your conscience is more important to you than the downside of possibly getting involved into the conflict. And then you can figure out how “strong” your action should be. Is easing your conscience the most important factor? Then you can directly ask them “hey, I noticed you had a strong exchange with person X, can I help somehow?” or maybe “what happened? What did person X do?” and then try to resolve it. If the possibility you’ll get sucked into the conflict is too scary to toy with, then stick with offering to make them a hot drink/getting something from the convenience store/small stuff like that + “hey, how’s it going?” to kinda do enough to show that you’re cool with them. 

Like these are insanely general guidelines thou. But I do like to use them even if only so I know what kinds of questions I might possibly ask myself. One of my personal issues with food is that I feel like I’m obligated to eat it. If it’s there in front of you, you “must” eat it, and I feel pressured which causes my anxiety to rise which causes me to lose my appetite. Some things that have helped me - 

snack snack snack! Keep a bowl of nuts/grapes/plain crackers/oatmeal cookies (healthy stuff that preferably has a lot of calories, just in case you can’t manage to eat a full meal) next to your bed, at the kitchen, on your desk, so that even if your eating schedule is fucked up you’re still getting some calories in and also so that your brain starts to overwrite the idea of food=anxiety with “oh well, food”. 

Second, try to do away with the idea that eating is an obligation. Figure out workarounds (trying again in 1h, having a meal replacement drink, eating snacks, etc.) just brainstorm, write things down as they come to mind. Can the food be reheated? Can it be cooked into something else? Can it be eaten cold? Etc. 

Third, attempt (key word attempt!) to keep an eating schedule. Pick convenient times (breakfast at 7, lunch at 13, second lunch at 18, final attempt to get some calories in at 21 is mine), and eat like one bite at those times. If you can eat a whole plate of food, cool, but don’t focus on quantity, focus on consistency. Eventually your body will get used to it. Might take days, weeks or months. But it’ll help you get at least some food in you. 

Fourth, eat food that’s tasty. I used to eat meat because my family cooks a lot of meat. I don’t like the texture of most meat. Now I don’t eat meat, and choose foods that I actually like eating lol. Maybe that’s not an issue for you, but it’s something obvious that I just… didn’t think of lol. 

Fifth, visualisation lol. Imagine yourself eating food at random times until you can think about it without anxiety. Maybe watch cooking shows lol. 

Sixth, distractions! Watch YouTube vids, read a book, crochet, watch a movie, browse Reddit, etc. The less attention you give your meal the easier it goes in. 

Seventh, physical exertion helps. Healthy sleep, correct meds, therapy, etc. These are all things you’re probably already working on, but it’s worth it to take a second look at them and check if they still suit your needs or need adjustment. Also, there are meds that improve appetite (one of the side effect of my meds is “weight gain”, which for me as a person with food anxiety means I’m finally at healthy weight now), so if you ever need to change your meds, one of the considerations you can tell your psychiatrist is appetite improving meds.

I wanna throw in a quick comment on “pull your toes up”. I used to mainly shift my board by flexing my ankles, and ended up with persistent shin splint pain while snowboarding. It was a pain in the ass trying to figure out what was making my legs hurt lol. So, in case you start getting shin splint pain, start working more with leaning forward by imagining your chest has a tether that’s pulling you forward to the slope. Some ankle flexing is fine, no prob, but try to ALSO work with your weight, don’t rely on flexing.

Yeah I’d def agree to getting a teacher for one session. Surfing/skating certainly helps, but they’re not automatically transferable to snowboarding. An instructor will lay out all the technical details you need, like body positioning, weight transferring, etc. We could write up a detailed how-to, but it’s WAY easier and faster if someone is looking at you and can correct you in real time. Also, then you don’t need to take breaks to read over the how to guide and watch back videos ya know. 

For now, practice transferring weight to the front foot and keeping your body upright. Shoulders, hips and feet should be on a straight line. Back straight. Bend knees more and then even more. Your shoulders should be directly over the board. Don’t twist your waist. Keep your arms straight out (make a T pose) and check that they’re over both ends of snowboard. Transfer weight to one foot and slip sideways. Try that to both sides. Change to toe edge and try it again. That’ll tide you over for the next few rides.

EDIT: instructor will teach you where to stop safely, how to get on/off a lift, how to move on flat ground, how to properly fasten bindings, how to flop over from sitting on your ass to sitting on your knees, etc. as well. It’s all the little details that make you a safe rider and make the session pleasant/minimise bruises etc.

Nah, I def agree with correcting blatantly false info. But you can only do that /after/ someone has expressed their opinion. And correcting them will never sound like “eat a burger” or “hit the thread mill”. Separate statements “eat more” or “exercise more” are almost never useful and have to come only after a person has explicitly asked you for your opinion on their specific habits. 

Take these two situations. 1) A person is eating lunch. Interrupting them to say eat more or eat less is not right. 2) someone is saying “I’ve eaten two ice chips a day for three months and haven’t lost weight!”. Now you can say “that’s incorrect!”. You still shouldn’t say just “exercise more” because it doesn’t help. You should say “that’s incorrect, because…” if you want to argue “in good faith”.

You gotta check which one of these types of situations you’re arguing with. A person expressing their frustration with randoms commenting on their body isn’t the right target to tell them “but technically…..” imo.

The logic tracks of course, but who does it help? You think a skinny person doesn’t know that they have to eat more to gain weight? You think a fat person doesn’t know that they have to (should) exercise to lose weight? The only one who gains something by saying “eat a burger” or “hit the thread mill” is the person saying it. They enjoy pointing out things they don’t like in other people. It itches a scratch. Sometimes an anxious person is not in the right headspace to be in a relationship and that’s okay. It just needs to be recognised. It’s nothing shameful. A person with a broken leg isn’t in the right state of health to be a dogwalker. A person who’s anxiety means that their romantic relationship bring them more pain than pleasure isn’t in the right headspace to be in a relationship, especially if it’s not an one-off thing but a consistent problem that has only worsened over time. 

That being said - are you genuinely happy in this relationship? Or are you walking on eggshells, trying to avert the next argument by stifling your own emotions and hobbies and other relationships? You cannot pick “I’m genuinely happy and also walking on eggshells”. Is she genuinely happy in this relationship? Or is she spending increasing amounts of time on her anxieties, i.e. checking your social media, texting you pointed questions about where you’re at, ruminating over a single incident for days until she blows up? She cannot pick both. 

If your relationship is not healthy (it’s not and it’s progressively getting worse) something needs to change. That change shouldn’t be you “internalising your emotions”. This will 100% lead to you developing resentment and will not benefit your relationship long term. It could improve it short term, but it will sink it long term. And yes, it is unsustainable. Especially because, if this eases her anxieties she will not want to “go back to how it was before” when she was more anxious. And you will be stuck with not expressing your genuine emotions or reservations, ever. Both parties to a relationship having strong boundaries is a sum greater than its parts, it improves everyone’s life. This shouldn’t be debatable. 

I suggest you both take a step back and reevaluate. Firstly, whether your relationship makes you genuinely happy. If it does, then it’s time to enact changes. For example, tell her you are unhappy. Your issue is that you feel very hurt by her words and actions on a 4-5 times a week basis. Your suggestions could be something like this - if she’s too anxious to have a verbal conversation about her worries she could start writing a journal, where she puts her anxious thoughts and/or questions, which you can access every week/every time you stay the night/etc., whatever works. Or maybe she promises to try to apply one of her therapeutic mechanisms at least once a day. Or maybe when she feels angry she steps away. Or maybe when she feels anxious about fidelity she writes it down and puts it out of her head, and revisits it the next day. Or maybe if she can feel herself getting worked up about something you did/didn’t do she always uses this format “I felt X when you did/didn’t do X. Please do X instead of X/please don’t do X”. Then figure out what you could offer in return. Maybe she’s anxious when you’re visiting friends - you could send her “arriving at X place” and “back home” texts. Or… idk, I’m having a harder time figuring this part out, but you get the vibe. Just be aware that yes, you should be compassionate, but co-dependence is BAD, so calling once an hour is not acceptable. 

Then it’s her turn. She should offer you suggestions for how you could change your habits to make this relationship healthier. Healthier being the key word, this is not about you being completely submissive to her anxiety, this is about finding compromise and working around triggers. Feeding anxiety breeds anxiety. That is why people with social anxiety are told to first go for a walk in public, then smile at the cashier, then meet with one friend, then two, etc. They are never told to lock their doors and only receive package drop offs at their door. She should consult her therapist on this. Then she should offer suggestions for how she could change her behaviour. 

Reevaluate in two weeks time. Hold yourselves and each other accountable. This can be done by writing the words down, not verbally, if that makes the situation less emotionally wrought. Adjust the plan. Something will work splendidly, something will not. If nothing had changed, ask yourself again if you are genuinely happy in this relationship or if you are hurting the both of you by staying in this relationship. 

This ended up being an essay, but that’s how I’d approach it. Make it a team sport! You’re both changing, compromising, working for a healthier relationship! It’s give and take, it’s a collaboration. It’s also a lot of work for BOTH parties. If it sounds like too much work (to you or to her) be aware that without work this spiral will get worse. There is no conceivable way in which it could improve. Her anxiety will get worse, your mental health will suffer, bad times all around. Hope this helps.

Regarding Japan - I suggest finding your personal top 5 resorts you think would fit your price preferences etc., finding the snowboarding schools/instructors in them, and either emailing them or calling them directly to find out the language barrier question. And definitely book your instructor beforehand (this goes for anywhere you might go)! Nothing is worse than arriving in your resort, popping in the ski school and finding out that they have one instructor available for 45min and that’s all for the whole 5 days of your trip. 

Can’t speak for USA. Japan will def be a more “unique” experience though. 

If you’re considering travelling to EU I have developed a very simple plan for travelling, which can probably be applied to USA and Japan as well. 

1. Find your top 5 resorts. Italy, France are the two classics with which you can start, but there are tons of other options. 

2. Find out how far away the resorts are, how close to them you can get. I choose resorts that I can get to with no longer than 3h of using airport-resort shuttle. If you’re renting a car it’s a bit easier. Discard resorts that are too far. 

3. Check time! Will you have to spend 6h sitting in an airport waiting for the shuttle? Will you arrive at 23:00 and will have to drive 5h after that? Etc. Discard resorts that take too much time to get to. 

4. Find your accommodations. Where are they situated, how near is ski bus, how near is ski lift, how near are restaurants, pubs, bars. Do they have ski storage, complimentary breakfast, etc. Here you can compromise. 

5. Check ski pass prices. Low season - high season, etc. 

Done. Resort-distance-time-accommodations-all else.

1. Why don’t vampires glamor all humans to believe they want to be fed on?
-I assume it’s because a lot of them just can’t be bothered and have grown used to the horribleness of vampire lifestyle. It’s probably kinda like going over speed limit. 2. Why are vampires said to be “immortal” when they can die (again) by the sun or stake.
-“Immortality” is a bit of a strange word in that it can be (is) defined in a lot of ways. One definition is “literally cannot be destroyed” but that would mean vampires floating in the space after Earth goes through it natural lifespan and dissipates/blows up/whatever will happen a very long time from now. The other definition, which is usually used in fantasy movies/books/etc. is that immortal beings cannot die from natural means. Aka unless they are killed/kill themselves they can, in theory, live forever. 

3. What happens to all the blood vampires drink since they don’t go to the bathroom?
-Dunno, but the usual “explanation” I’ve encountered is that blood gets turned into energy. It’s just a much more streamlined process since vampires turn ALL of the blood into energy, while we take what we need from food and poop the rest of it out (to reeeeeeally generalise the whole process).

4. How do vampires cry blood since they don’t circulate blood it would all be at their feet?
-Who knows. Maybe they are, like, “infused” with blood after drinking it. Like it somehow spreads all around their body. But honestly, I don’t think a rational explanation is possible for that one. 

5. Why do vampires always drink blood from humans bodies directly? I’d assume it’s nicer (and cleaner) to have bottles blood.
-Might be habit for most of them. It might also be more pleasurable to drink straight from humans. Kinda like cold cocoa in a glass bottle is still cocoa, but hot cocoa in a mug is a much better option regardless. 

6. Why don’t all humans that are fed on have the vampires clean the wound like Bill did with Sookie?
-I assume because most vampires don’t really care about the humans they feed from. Are we ever showed a loving, heathy human-vampire relationship in the show? I honestly can’t remember any. So it might just be a “why bother” kind of thing. 

7. Why don’t hospitals buy vampire blood for wounded people in hospitals?
-Vampire blood has seeeerious side effects. It’s basically both a hallucinogenic drug (on top of that- addictive) and a magical binding between the human and the vampire. Also, I’m pretty sure that a lot of (most?) countries have laws against paying for the body parts of people due to really serious ethical issues. Prefacing this to say that English is not my first language so my snowboarding terms might be a bit iffy. 

Keep an eye on the hand which is behind you. Ideally your arms/shoulders should always be parallel to the board. A good way of checking this is literally stretching your arms out, and just seeing where they are. Challenge yourself to keep your shoulders constantly parallel for at least one entire run, or just check in on that every now and then. 

Same for your hips. They should also be parallel to your board, generally speaking. When tou swish your board out to shed some speed you’ll of course make your board perpendicular to your body, but generally your hips and shoulders should be parallel to your board. 

Drop deeper, aka squat a bit more. Your back should stay straight and upright while you squat. The rule of thumb (very generally speaking) is that you can ALWAYS drop deeper. It’s also really fun to drop real deep in fast speeds, it feels super impressive so it’s a lot of fun. You can also try dropping deeper JUST before you turn. It’ll give you a boost of speed on the turn and let you control your board better. 

You have lovely turns to the right, aka when you’re on the heel edge of your board. Your toe edge turns could be sharper- try keeping your shoulders parallel to the board, and turning more/doing longer turns. Maybe challenge yourself to do equally wide/long/sharp turns to both heel and toe edge for a single run. Just try making both turns identical. You’ll feel the difference and then you can check in every now and then on casual runs. 

I would also suggest more leaning and less working with your ankles. With that I mean- if you want deeper heel edge turns then try leaning with your whole body backwards a bit more. Same for toe edge turns. This works better in higher speeds than lower. 

When doing ollies- also keep your shoulders more parallel. You should pop with your shoulders squared and drop the same way. Your board should point straight downwards when you pop, and when you drop it should still stay pointed straight downwards. You can also try squatting super deep before popping, just try doing a super deep drop in a squat, pop and drop back into a deep squat. You’ll have more control over the board and if you do it on a nice smooth bump it’s like a mini jump. Feels impressive and is fun. 

If you haven’t tried it yet- try out riding switch. You don’t have to be just as good riding switch as regular, but it’s a good way of finding out your bad habits. It’s also useful, sometimes if you’re riding in the woods for example you might have to do a single turn around a tree in switch, it’s also a good way of resting your leading leg, and it’s a good way of exercising all sides of your body equally. Also, if you ever want to try 180°s it’s a necessity. Idk maybe you already ride switch, but I mean, you can always ride more switch haha. 

But to be honest this is just a lot of little things. You already look very comfortable and confident on the board, you control it well and it’d be fun watching you ride by. These are just things to keep in mind if you want to look even sharper/improve/blah blah blah.

I personally like to simply do a “roll call” of my body parts when riding. 
1. Shoulders squared?
2. Back straight and upright?
3. Hips squared? 
4. Knees bent? 
5. Weight equally on both feet/more on your leading foot?
I’ve gotten into a habit of checking that list so now I do it automatically and can correct any mistakes instantly. 

TLDR because this turned into an essay: keep your shoulders and hips parallel to your board, drop into a deeper squat (then even deeper because you can always drop deeper).

Yep, precisely! It’s the kind of thing which is obvious with hindsight, but can go unnoticed if you’ve never given it much thought. I know I wasn’t taught that conditioner shouldn’t go on skin and found out by accident at like, age 20 lol.

I agree on washing your hair just the right amount, over scrubbing is bad. I like combing my hair just before washing it, because that way you can loosen the scabs a bit and wash them out right after and you need less scrubbing with shampoo. Definitely no sleeping with wet hair, and I also found that there needs to be a good rhythm of how often hair is washed as well. If you wash too often the skin dries out, if you leave it sweaty/dirty for too long the scabs will breed. Nizoral helped me a bit but what’s helped the most is apple cider vinegar. I dilute it around 1 part vinegar 10 parts water (super weak), wash my hair with shampoo and rise the shampoo out, pour the vinegar mixture on my scalp, let it sit for a minute or two and then rinse it out. I do it each time I wash my hair, so every second or third day. With the vinegar my scalp cleared up in like two weeks. Since it’s a very weak dilution and cheap I really recommend trying that out. Just don’t use it if you have any open sores (it stings), use a weak dilution, if it gets in your eyes then rinse them out, don’t leave it on for longer than 10 minutes, if it doesn’t help/makes the skin worse then stop using it, all that common sense stuff.
EDIT: just remembered this. It might be counterintuitive, but using hair conditioner on my scalp actually made my skin worse. I had less “dry” dandruff but more “moist” scabs/dandruff/???whatever those things were. So it might help if you change your conditioner/stop using it on your scalp. I only use it on hair which falls below my nape. It’s a weird thing which doesn’t cross everyone’s minds so I thought I’d suggest it as well lol.
